blocks.text: Chapter 7
PRATIJÑĀ
A brilliant example of the timely relevance!

Just as Bhīṣma, Bhīma, Gāndhārī, Arjuna, and numerous other characters gave their solemn words, so too have we. Was their commitment worthwhile? Is it worth clinging onto? These archetypes serve as a beacon of light, illuminating our fleeting existence.
Chapter 8
KARṆA - THE MAESTRO WHO WENT WIDE OF THE MARK

Karṇa epitomizes the confluence of right and wrong, virtue and vice in human nature. Nevertheless, the path of Dharma is the only way forward - no shortcuts, no excuses. In Mahābhārata, we may find a part of ourselves in all the characters. Let us learn from their mistakes and avoid similar errors in our own lives.

header: A Timeless Itihāsa for Timely Needs

blocks.text: the Bhagavadgītā, then he can do better carpentry.

This is the greatness of Mahābhārata. It is an open text. It is a timely and timeless text. Let us not forget that ultimately it is a sacred text that aims at Mokṣa. It is a Mokṣa śāstra. And if we are going to concentrate only on the social, sociological, or ethnological aspects, then we are missing out on the core. We are only talking about the chemical composition of Shakespeare’s ink. We are not talking about the play. You have to immerse yourself in Mahābhārata. You have to allow Mahābhārata to fill you with its fundamental values.
Chapter 7
PRATIJÑĀ

Embarking on the journey of Mahābhārata is in itself experiencing the physical presence of the divine in our life. The accounts of Bhagavān Kṛṣṇa, Maharṣi Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa, Bhārgavarāma, Balarāmā, Devavrata-Bhīṣma or Maharṣi Animāndavyā, among many more, are awe-inspiring moments of reading. When Devavrata makes that fierce and terrible vow, the skies thunder with the voices of the Gods, "Bhīṣma... Bhīṣma...". When the Pāṇḍavas are born, all the devas appear in the sky and shower them with blessings and flowers (Whereas when Duryodhana is born, a donkey brays outside, and the minster suggests that this being a bad sign, he should be abandoned then and there to save the kingdom).

Animāndavyā Muni, mistaken to be part of a group of thieves, gets caught by the King's soldiers, and is punished. He bears the pain of being held up on a spear to the spine, without dying, while the other thieves die. The king realises

his mistake later, and releases him, yet the spear could not be removed. And he lives out his life with the spear still intact. When finally he reaches the abode of Yama-Dharma, Yamadeva himself gets cursed by Animāṇḍavyā Muni for misinterpreting Dharma, which led to this ill fate. Even Dharmadeva himself is not above Dharma.

Mahābhārata presents to us, logic, decisions, contexts, characters, feelings, and emotions, that are complex to figure out. A student of this grand Itihāsa is forced to grind and churn his heart and mind, which itself becomes a process that earns an understanding of Dharma.

In the Ādi Parva, Devavrata spontaneously decides and proclaims the Bhīṣma-Pratijñā, and becomes Bhīṣma. And we began to wonder if it was the right thing to do. Surely, it was not the case that his father Śantanu's life depended on it. The future of the kingdom did not depend on it! His own life too did not depend on it! The Pratijñā only catered to his father's kāma.

Devavrata, appointed yuvarāja of the Kuru dynasty, learns of his father's love for Satyavatī. To marry her, Śantanu must fulfil Satyavatī's father's conditions, which include making Satyavatī's son the next king. Śantanu rejects this proposal. But later Devavrata accepts, without seeking counsel. To make this happen he takes a lifelong vow of Brahmacarya and renounces his claim to the throne. He earns the name Bhīṣma, 'the one of the Terrible Vow', and the power to choose the time of his death. As we begin learning Mahābhārata, we are
thrust into finding logic and reason here, weighing the need for such a pratijñā against its consequences.

This decision to renounce a key administrative post without notice or consultation raises questions about its Dharma. As Yuvarāja, didn't Devavrata have a higher responsibility to seek his father's permission? What was the drive behind Bhīṣma's decision to take this lifelong vow of celibacy, without any thought for its impact on the kingdom? How could Bhīṣma be certain that Satyavatī would bear children? And if she did, would they be capable of becoming morally and intellectually qualified kings?

Satyavatī does give birth to two sons. But ironically, both of them passed away without having any children. The younger son, Vicitravīrya, died leaving behind two widows, Ambikā and Ambālikā. As per the Vedic tradition, a widow of an heirless king is allowed to bear a child with a suitable surrogate. Satyavatī asks Bhīṣma to do it. And she even asks him to take the throne and be king. Bhīṣma disagreed to both proposals.

Here we wonder again. Śāntanu has died. Satyavatī's children too have died. The only person who is left behind, who is a stakeholder to the Bhīṣma-pratijñā is Satyavatī. And she is proposing that Bhīṣma forfeit his vow, and take back the kingdom. Satyavatī may have been ambitious before, in wanting to be the rājamātā. Bhīṣma's vow ensured this. But now even Satyavatī is able to see that it was all in vain. She embraced the intelligent way out of this predicament. Yet Bhīṣma rejects! Why? For whose benefit?

Maharṣi Vyāsa, another son of Satyavatī, fathered children with the widows, leading to the birth of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura. Adding to the previous irony, both Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu were considered unfit to be the King. And another was born, Vidura, but to a maid. Though he was exemplary, he too could not be the King. Pāṇḍu was chosen and he ruled well, only to die too soon, with heirs not old enough. The throne is left empty yet again.

This throne finds a stable king only at the end of the Kurukṣetra war. Though Yudhiṣṭira becomes king in between, he is unseated by Duryodhana's wicked plots. Now one has to wonder, "Was this pratijñā so important?" How many people may have suffered from this continued kinglessness? In the end, 18 akṣauhiṇīs of soldiers died in battle.

This much hailed Pratijñā, has many nuances. On the one hand, it is a tremendous feat, impossible for most men. Even Ārjuna couldn’t keep to his twelve year Brahmacarya, when he was exiled for walking in on Yudhiṣṭira and Draupadī. The sharp contrast to Bhīṣma’s brahmacarya is his own father’s weakness that drew him to Satyavatī. We also see how King Mahābhiṣā (who was born as Śantanu as per Bhagavān Brahma’s instruction) was drawn to Gaṅgādevī as well. Hence there is no doubt that Bhīṣma is the Brahmacarya archetype of Mahābhārata.

Such strength and willpower could have taken Bhāratavarṣa a long way, had it been used for the needs of the kingdom. Unfortunately, we can only imagine how the kingdom could have been had Devavrata ruled as king. Bound by his Pratijñā, Bhīṣma became powerless even before a blind king and his son.

Bhīṣma is indeed the archetype of a Brahamacari in Mahābhārata. But is he the archetype of Dharma or Pratijñā? When our vows contradict Dharma, what should we do? Let us explore Mahābhārata further for the Pratijñā archetype.

We focus on the vows taken by a few characters from Mahābhārata - Gāndhārī, Ārjuna , and Bhīma. We will study the circumstances under which the Pratijñās were taken and the consequences that followed. We will also draw a parallel to our present-day lives, understanding the Pratijñās we take.
Gāndhārī’s Pratijñā
Gāndhārī was the daughter of King Subala from Gandhāradeśa. King Subala had many sons, the eldest being

Śakuni. Bhīṣma was in search of a suitable bride for the blind prince Dhṛtarāṣṭra. When he heard of Princess Gāndhārī, he sent a messenger to King Subala asking for his daughter's hand in marriage to Dhṛtarāṣṭra. King Ṣubala hesitated at first as Prince Dhṛtarāṣṭra was blind. However, he later agreed considering the greatness of the Kurus and Bhīṣma.

Gāndhārī, on hearing that her parents had arranged her marriage to the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra, picked up a piece of cloth and blindfolded herself. As her husband was blind, she decided resolutely that she would never experience more than her husband could. Such was her dedication towards her husband that she chose to stand behind him in every sense.

This act of hers has received plentiful praise. But was it the right choice? Modern-day scholars raise a pertinent question, whether the most important thing in a marriage is the evenness of the husband and wife or their compatibility. Shouldn't both partners complement each other as they walk the householder's life?

No matter how much we eulogise her, this hasty Pratijñā certainly has had deep repercussions. Duryodana's stubbornness and inflated ego were never corrected and improper parenting had the lion's share of contribution in the upbringing of some of the most unprincipled characters of the Itihāsa. The choice to keep her eyes closed also has an inner connotation - to turn a blind eye to all the activities done by her sons. Undeniably, the role of the mother is paramount when raising children. The situation might have
been different if she had not blindfolded herself, and become the eyes for her husband instead.

Amma says, "The principle of motherhood is as vast and powerful as the universe. With the power of motherhood within her, a woman can influence the entire world". In Gāndhārī's case, we see her failing to influence her children for the better. Her Pratijñā to remain blindfolded arose not from the clarity of thinking but more from an instantaneous emotional response, at an age when she would have had relatively less understanding about the essence, purpose, and comprehensiveness of marriage.
Arjuna's Pratijñā
Arjuna's Pratijñā was to kill Jayadratha before sunset. During the Kurukṣetra war, Arjuna's son Abhimanyu was killed on the thirteenth day, which led to this vow.

Droṇācārya constructed a deadly army formation called Cakravyūha. The Pāṇḍavas planned that Abhimanyu would penetrate the army formation, while the other warriors would follow and protect him. But King Jayadratha's unexpected interference prevented the rest of the Pāṇḍava warriors from entering the Cakravyūha. Abhimanyu, however, breached the army formation and killed Duryodhana's son and many other princes. Sadly, breaking all the ethics of Dharmayuddha, Abhimanyu was simultaneously attacked by many powerful warriors of Duryodhana's army. He was killed by a final blow from Duhśāsana son. When Arjuna learned of his son's death, he was filled with anger, and he pledged that he would kill Jayadratha the very next day before sunset.

Duryodhana, on hearing Arjuna’s Pratijñā, consulted his advisors to come up with a plan to prevent Arjuna from killing Jayadratha in battle. Droṇācārya arranged a combination of three vyūhas (military formations) in order to protect Jayadratha from Arjuna. Bhīma, Sātyaki, and Arjuna tore through the Kaurava army but Jayadratha was hiding behind Droṇācārya, and it became very evident that Arjuna would not be able to kill Jayadratha before sunset. But Bhagavān Śrī Kṛṣṇa came to his rescue. Bhagavān sent his Sudarśanacakra to mask the sun and create the illusion of sunset. Jayadratha came out thinking the sun had set and that the Pratijñā had been forfeited. Bhagavān withdrew his Sudarśanachakra, revealing the sun. Seizing this opportunity Arjuna picked up his Gāṇḍīva and killed Jayadratha with the Pāśupatāstra.

Here we can see, Arjuna’s Pratijñā did not arise from clear thought. Rather it was an emotional response to the anger he felt, learning of his son’s death by adharma. Meanwhile, the Kauravas had planned well to defend Jayadratha from Arjuna and they would have succeeded if it was not for Bhagavān’s intervention.
Bhīma’s Pratijñā

Duryodhana, influenced by his uncle Śakuni, invited the Pāṇḍavas for a game of dice. Śakuni resorted to deceit, defeated Yudhiṣṭhira, and won his possessions one by one. Yudhiṣṭhira lost everything; his army, kingdom, his brothers, and himself to Duryodhana, and, finally even their wife
Draupadī.

As Draupadī was forcefully pulled by her hair into the sabhā, Duhśāsana attempted to disrobe her, but she was saved by Bhagavān Kṛṣṇa. Bhīma, overflowing with rage, vowed to kill Duhśāsana in war, to tear open his chest and drink his blood. Draupadī was further vilified by Karṇa and Duryodhana. Duryodhana taunted Draupadī by gesturing to her to come and sit on his thigh, indicating her servitude to him. Bhīma, infuriated, made a second Pratijñā that he would break Duryodhana's thigh in battle.
Like the other Pratijñā's we discussed so far, Bhīma too took these vows reacting to his emotions. However, these Pratijñās are markedly different - let us see how.

In Udyoga Parva, we see the Pāṇḍavas requesting their kingdom back from the Kauravas, as agreed in the 'Game of Dice'. Duryodhana however, refuses this request and all other requests made by the Pāṇḍavas. Though war seemed inevitable, Bhagavān Kṛṣṇa went as a peace messenger to the court of the Kauravas to negotiate a peaceful resolution to the conflict with Duryodhana. Kṛṣṇa consulted all the five Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī before his journey to meet Duryodhana. Surprisingly, Bhīma approved of peace rather than war, just like his elder brother Yudhiṣṭira. He was willing to forgo his Pratijñās to kill Duryodhana and Duhśāsana. Here we see that he did not ponder the question of war or peace in light of the Pratijñā he made.
But, war became inevitable no matter how hard Bhagavān

tried. Bhīma fulfils his first Pratijñā, and kills Duḥśāsana in battle, without conflicting Dharma. Towards the end of the war, the Kaurava army was reduced to Duryodhana, Ashwatthāma, Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarma. When Duryodhana was given the option to choose any one of the Pāṇḍava warriors for a one-on-one battle, he picked Bhīma and suggested a mace fight. The fight continued for a long time and Bhīma started getting tired. Observing this, Kṛṣṇa signalled Bhīma to strike Duryodhana hard on his thigh and break it. Bhīma followed Bhagavān's instructions and defeated Duryodhana. Here we see that Bhīma chose to fight and defeat Duryodhana in full adherence to dharma. His Pratijñā to break Duryodhana's thigh does not interfere with his dharmic acumen. When he did break his thigh in the end, it was only to fulfil Bhagavān's instruction and not his Pratijñā. Though Bhīma ended up making Pratijñā's out of anger, he did not let it cloud his judgement or his decisions.

All three Pratijñās were emotionally based. Gāndhārī's Pratijñā, though considered noble, blinded her to the adharma of her children. This adharma grew day by day and eventually resulted in the bloodshed of the entire family alongside countless others. Arjuna's Pratijñā could have gotten him in a fix since he took the vow without any forethought. But thanks to Kṛṣṇa he could fulfil it. Bhīma while taking the Pratijñā was in an emotionally challenging situation but was willing to prioritise Dharma. This is evident from his opinion to opt for peace over war. It is also
evident from his battle with Duryodhana.

Don't we all take such Pratijñās in our daily lives when we find ourselves in some emotional situations? Sometimes consciously and sometimes subconsciously without even realising it, we take vows. "I won't talk to that person", silent treatments, "I won't do this or that anymore", etc. These are all different forms of Pratijñās.
Having taken such vows, there are two questions that we should contemplate.

The first one is whether we took the vow out of intellectual clarity or whether it was a spontaneous outburst in a demanding situation. If we took the Pratijñā as an emotional retort, then the second question after comprehending the bigger picture is whether there is any use in sticking to that Pratijñā. We should follow it if we still feel that the Pratijñā is beneficial for us or our society. Otherwise, shouldn't we drop it? Let us explore one more Pratijñā to understand.

Bhagavān Śrī Kṛṣṇa took a vow to not take up arms in the Kurukṣetra war. This was the condition he placed before Arjuna and Duryodhana. He said he would join on one side, and his army on the other, and that he would not carry or use weapons in battle. This led Duryodhana to take Śrī Kṛṣṇa's Yādava army. And Arjuna wholeheartedly welcomed Bhagavān to his side.
But in the war, Śrī Kṛṣṇa was forced to reconsider when Bhīṣma took a counter vow to make him do so. Bhīṣma's determination to destroy the Pāṇḍavas at any cost became
more and more apparent. And on the other side, Arjuna's reverence for Bhīṣma kept holding him back from attacking with his full capacity. Śrī Kṛṣṇa could no longer allow it.

With a chariot wheel in hand, Kṛṣṇa dashed towards Bhīṣma. It was only Arjuna's promise to fight to the best of his ability that pacified him. Śrī Kṛṣṇa spoke clearly to Bhīṣma, telling him that he was misusing his boon of choosing his hour of death against warriors who had no such mystical protection.

Here you find that Bhagavān Kṛṣṇa was not tied by his Pratijñā. It did not hold him back or make him hesitate. With clarity, he took to action answering the call of Dharma. Bhagavān himself is the Pratijñā archetype in Mahābhārata, revealing to us much more about Bhīṣma who trapped himself with his Pratijñā, unable to respond to adharma.
Chapter 8
KARṆA: THE MAESTRO WHO WENT WIDE OF THE MARK

Karṇa has been one of the most debated characters in Mahābhārata. There are different versions of his story; hence, an overall understanding of his character has become vague. Literary works like Bhāsa's Karṇabhāram, Mṛtyunjaya by Śivajī Sawanth and other writers and scholars, "piece together from segments" where Karṇa becomes the main character (Hiltebeitel, 2011, p.484). There are a lot of explanations justifying Karṇa's fall from dhārmic ethics and principles, to unrighteousness and evil. Those who side with Karṇa claim his superiority over Arjuna in instances where the latter failed to resist the Nāgāstra on the seventeenth day of the Kurukṣetra battle (and Kṛṣṇa saving Arjuna). The fact is that in a war, even the mightiest warrior will have their moments of failure and Karṇa cannot be labelled as superior because of this. After all, he was not the only warrior who
